protocols.name: Building a new habit
protocols.when: When your goal is something you want to do regularly: move, write, save, wake earlier.
steps: Name it as who you’re becoming, plus one tiny action: “I’m someone who moves every day. Shoes on, ten minutes.”
Shrink it until it survives a Tuesday. If it feels too small, it’s probably the right size.
Anchor it to something you already do, not to a clock: after coffee, after the school run, before your phone.
Write three versions: for a good day, an okay day and a hard day. All three count.
Do it most days, at whatever moment works that day.
Write one line a day about what you actually did.
Missed a day? No catch-up. Come back the next day, and try not to miss twice in a row.
Every 7 days, look back: keep it, shrink it or change its shape. Grow it one notch only when it feels easy most days.
signals: Your goal is something to do regularly: move, write, save, wake earlier.
You keep restarting the same habit.
protocols.start: Week 1: name it and shrink it, plus the tiny daily version. Nothing else.
protocols.deeper: Week 3 on: add the anchor, the three versions and the weekly look back. Grow it one notch only when it feels easy most days.
working: You do some version most days without being reminded.
Misses are single days, not runs of days.
protocols.done: When it happens most days without much effort for about four weeks. Then it becomes background, and a new goal can start.

protocols.name: Unlearning an old habit
protocols.when: When your goal is about stopping something that’s costing you: scrolling, snacking, procrastinating, overworking.
steps: Notice without judging. For three days, write down when it happens: what set it off, how you felt, what you got from it.
Find the payoff. Ask: what am I getting out of this? Relief, comfort, a break, a sense of control.
Make the old way a little harder. Move it, log out, put it in another room, add a step between you and it.
Choose a swap that gives you the same payoff in a better way: a walk for the break, a text to a friend for the comfort.
When the urge shows up, pause for two minutes and feel it before you choose. Urges rise, and they pass.
A slip is information. Write what set it off and what would help next time, then carry on.
Tell one person in your circle what you’re changing, and ask them to check in.
Count the days you chose differently, not the days you didn’t.
protocols.safety: If the habit involves alcohol, drugs, gambling, food, self-harm or anything that puts you in danger, this doesn’t replace real help. Talk to a doctor or counselor. If you’re in crisis, call your local emergency number or a crisis line now.
signals: Your goal is about stopping something: scrolling, snacking, procrastinating, overworking.
You mention the same habit winning again and again.
protocols.start: Week 1: notice and track the trigger only. No changes yet.
protocols.deeper: Week 2 on: make the old way harder, add the swap, and use the slip debrief after any slip.
working: You can name your triggers and the payoff.
The time between slips gets longer.
protocols.done: When the old habit is rare and the swap feels normal. Keep the slip debrief for the odd hard day.

protocols.name: Clearing your field
protocols.when: When something in your life keeps pulling against your goal: a person, a habit, a food, a feed, a place, a commitment. Let loose, but be precise about what you let in.
steps: Take stock of what you let in: people, places, habits, food, feeds, commitments. Mark each one: gives energy, drains it, or neither.
For each drain, ask: does this help my goal or cost it? Be honest, not harsh.
Choose the gentlest change that works: less of it, a boundary around it, or letting it go. Most things need a boundary, not a slammed door.
With people, start with a kind, clear boundary: “I can’t talk after 9.” Distance comes before goodbye. With anyone close, think it through first, and never cut someone off in the heat of the moment.
With habits and food, swap, don’t starve. Change one thing at a time and replace it with something that gives you what it gave you. No crash diets, no extreme cuts.
Clear one small space at a time: one drawer, one app, one feed. Unfollow, mute, delete.
Fill the space you made with something that feeds your goal. Empty space fills back up with the old thing.
Letting go has a price too. Grief or guilt can show up, even for the right change. After 7 days, check in: lighter, or lonelier? Adjust from there.
protocols.safety: If someone in your life is unsafe or harming you, get support from someone you trust or a professional before you act, and if you’re in danger, call your local emergency number or a domestic violence hotline. Before big changes to food, alcohol, medication or other substances, talk to a doctor.
signals: You describe a person, feed, food or commitment that keeps pulling against your goal.
You feel drained without knowing why.
protocols.start: Week 1: the field check only. See what’s there before changing anything.
protocols.deeper: Week 2 on: one boundary or one cleared space at a time, then fill the gap.
working: More energy, or less dread, in the parts of the week you changed.
Your boundaries hold without a fight.
protocols.done: Ongoing and light: a field check once a month.

protocols.name: The Price check: when it gets hard
protocols.when: When you’ve stalled, pushed back or missed several days, or you say the goal feels wrong. The Price stage of your goal.
steps: Pause before deciding. Feel what’s there first: tired, scared, bored, or something deeper.
Remember that resistance doesn’t automatically mean it’s wrong. Friction is part of how results happen.
Ask: is this friction or a signal? Friction sounds like “this is hard, and I still want it.” A signal sounds like “this costs me more than it gives,” every time.
Look back over the last 2 to 4 weeks: have doors been opening, or closing again and again? (See “Reading flow and resistance”.)
Ask yourself the Price question again: what would getting what you want actually cost you, and would you still pay that on a hard day?
If it’s friction, keep going, and shrink the step until it fits.
If it’s a signal, choose one: change the shape (same goal, different way), not now (pick a date to look again), or let it go with acceptance.
Whatever you choose, write one line on why. That’s data, not a verdict.
Letting go with acceptance isn’t giving up. It makes room for the next goal.
signals: You’ve missed several days in a row, or say the goal feels wrong.
Your check-ins sound stuck, heavy or resentful.
protocols.start: The pause, and the question: friction or signal?
protocols.deeper: Look back 2 to 4 weeks and choose: keep going, change the shape, not now, or let go.
working: You make a clear choice instead of drifting.
If you keep going, the step fits again.
protocols.done: Once a choice is made and written down. Revisit only on the date you set.

protocols.name: Tries and the data debrief
protocols.when: When you don’t know yet what you want, or want to test something before committing: a career, a hobby, a business idea, a new kind of relationship. Try more things sooner.
steps: Decide whether your goal is a Build (you know you want it) or a Try (you want to find out).
Give a Try a set length: 2 to 4 weeks. Long enough to learn, short enough to start now.
Pick what you’ll notice along the way: what you enjoy, what comes naturally, what drains you.
Do it for real, with small daily steps like any goal.
At the end, do the data debrief. Feel it first, then find the data.
Decide: turn it into a Build, run another Try, or close it and move on.
Add what you learned to your “What I’m learning about me” list.
Count every Try as a win. Each one moves you closer to what’s yours.
signals: You don’t know yet what you want.
You’re weighing a big change: a career, a business, a move.
protocols.start: Call it a Try, set the length, and pick what to notice.
protocols.deeper: Run it for real, then the full data debrief, and add to your “What I’m learning about me” list.
working: You finish Tries instead of quietly dropping them.
Your “learning about me” list keeps growing.
protocols.done: At the end of each Try, with a clear decision: Build, another Try, or close it.

protocols.name: Gut calls
protocols.when: When a step, or the whole plan, feels wrong in your gut.
steps: You know your life better than any method, this one included. If your gut says no, you can skip or change a step.
Make it a gut call on purpose: write what you’re skipping or changing, and what your gut is saying.
Then follow your gut fully. No half-measures.
In two weeks, look back: how did it play out?
Ask: was that my intuition, or fear in disguise? Intuition tends to feel calm and clear. Fear tends to feel urgent and tight.
Keep a gut record. Over time you’ll see when your gut is right, and when it’s protecting you from growing.
No shame either way. A gut call that went sideways is still data.
signals: You skip a step and say it felt wrong.
You say something like “something’s telling me…”.
protocols.start: Make one gut call on purpose, and write it down.
protocols.deeper: Check back at two weeks, and keep a gut record over the months.
working: You can tell more often whether it was intuition or fear.
You trust yourself faster.
protocols.done: Always available. The gut record keeps growing.

protocols.name: Receiving it
protocols.when: When you reach your goal, or a big part of it. The Receive stage of your goal.
steps: Stop and mark it. Say out loud what you did to get here.
On the day: write what changed in your life, your days, your body, your money and your relationships.
Notice what it drains and what it amplifies. More energy or less? More peace or more pressure?
Ask how it lands on the people around you: does it help them, cost them, or both?
Name what it costs to keep it. Every new level has upkeep.
At 30 days and again at 90 days, answer the same questions and compare.
Decide what to keep, adjust or let go. Then choose your next goal when you’re ready, not before.
signals: You say you reached your goal, or a big milestone.
protocols.start: Mark it, and write what changed.
protocols.deeper: The 30-day and 90-day reviews, then decide what to keep, adjust or let go.
working: You can name what it costs to keep, not only what it gave.
protocols.done: After the 90-day review. Then the next goal, when you’re ready.

protocols.name: Holding the new level
protocols.when: After you reach a goal, while life tests whether the change will stick. The Hold stage of your goal.
steps: Expect tests. A new level gets tested, often by the same thing in a new form.
Pick your own word for where tests come from: life, God, the universe, or just “things that happen”. The app will use yours.
When a test shows up, log it in one line: what happened.
Then ask: did I meet it with my old reaction, or a new response?
Old reaction? No shame. Notice what set it off, and what the new response would have been.
New response? Mark it. That’s the new level holding.
Watch for the same test coming back in a new form. Spotting it is half of handling it.
Each level asks something new of you: more time, more boundaries, more help. Update your load map and your circle.
signals: After a goal is reached.
You describe an old situation showing up again.
protocols.start: Pick your word for tests, and log the first test.
protocols.deeper: Spot the same test in new forms, and update your load and your circle.
working: More new responses than old reactions.
You spot repeat tests early.
protocols.done: When the new level feels normal. Tests still come; they just don’t knock you back.

protocols.name: Be precise: the word check
protocols.when: Whenever you write your goal or a check-in. The other half of “let loose”: live lightly, but be exact about the words you use for what matters.
steps: Read your goal out loud. Does every word say exactly what you mean?
Watch for loose words: “try to”, “maybe”, “I hope”, “someday”, “I never”, “I always”, “I can’t”.
Rewrite it to be exact and true. Not fake-positive, just precise. “I’ll try to run more” becomes “I run 10 minutes, 4 days a week.”
Name the thing, the amount and the when, if you can.
Say what you want, not only what you don’t. “Stop being broke” becomes “Have $2,000 saved by June.”
Swap “I never” and “I always” for what’s actually true: “I haven’t yet” or “I often”.
If the precise version feels scary to say, keep it anyway. Precise is a kind of honesty.
signals: Your goal is vague: “be happier”, “get healthy”, “make more money”.
Your check-ins use “try to”, “never”, “always”.
protocols.start: Rewrite the goal once, exact and true.
protocols.deeper: A weekly word check on your check-ins.
working: Your goal names the thing, the amount and the when.
protocols.done: When precise is your default. Then it’s a quick check at each new goal.

protocols.name: When you feel alone
protocols.when: When you feel lonely, disconnected, or like no one gets you, even with people around. The other side of “When it’s too much”.
steps: Name it without shame. Loneliness is a signal, like hunger: it means you need connection, not that something is wrong with you.
Notice which kind it is: missing closeness with someone, missing a group, or feeling unseen even around people.
Start small: one message to one person. “Thought of you today.”
Be around people with no pressure: a café, a class, a gym, a walk where others are.
Show up somewhere on a regular basis. Closeness grows from seeing the same faces again.
Let one person in a little more: share something real, and ask them something real back.
Check: solitude or isolation? Solitude is chosen and recharges you. Isolation drifts in and drains you.
protocols.safety: If loneliness turns into hopelessness, or thoughts of not wanting to be here, reach out now: to someone you trust, a doctor, or a crisis line. You don’t have to carry that alone.
signals: You mention feeling lonely, unseen, or having no one to tell.
Several check-ins in a row with no mention of other people.
protocols.start: Name it without shame, and send one small message.
protocols.deeper: Show up somewhere regularly, and let one person in a little more.
working: You have at least one regular face, and one person you can be real with.
protocols.done: When you feel connected most weeks. Check solitude or isolation once a month.

protocols.name: When it’s too much
protocols.when: When people, noise, screens, plans or other people’s needs leave you overloaded, wired or snappy. The other side of “When you feel alone”.
steps: Notice the signs: snappy, foggy, wired but tired, wanting everyone to stop talking.
Take a quiet reset: ten minutes with no input. No phone, no talk, no noise.
Cut one input today: notifications off, one plan moved, one group chat muted.
Say a kind no to one ask: “I can’t this week, but thank you for thinking of me.”
Protect your recharge: put alone time on your calendar like a meeting.
Use your senses to come down: a walk outside, a shower, dim lights, slow music.
Find your mix. Everyone needs a different amount of people and quiet. Notice yours, and plan your week around it.
Too much can tip into too little. If quiet turns into hiding, use “When you feel alone”.
signals: You describe being snappy, foggy, or wired but tired.
Several packed days in a row with no rest.
protocols.start: The quiet reset, and cut one input.
protocols.deeper: Protect recharge time every week, and find your own mix of people and quiet.
working: You notice overload earlier.
Your recharge time actually happens.
protocols.done: When your week has a rhythm with real quiet in it.

protocols.name: Opening doors: new people, new opportunities
protocols.when: When your goal needs people or chances you don’t have yet: work, clients, love, friends, mentors, ideas, money. Opportunities come in every form.
steps: Decide which doors you want opened: work, love, friendship, mentors, ideas, money.
Tell people your goal. Opportunities find people who say out loud what they’re looking for.
Walk into one new room a month: an event, a class, a group, a community online or in person, where people care about what you care about.
Give first. Share a lead, make an introduction, help with something small. Giving opens more doors than asking.
Reach out to one new or old contact a week. Keep it simple and real.
Follow up. Most doors open on the second or third conversation, not the first.
Say yes to an invite you’d usually skip, unless your gut says no.
Ask for one introduction: “Who do you know who…?”
Keep your field clear while it grows. New people are welcome, and your boundaries still count.
signals: Your goal needs people or chances you don’t have yet.
You feel stuck in the same circle.
protocols.start: Decide which doors, and tell three people your goal.
protocols.deeper: One new room a month, give first, and follow up.
working: New conversations, invites or offers start showing up.
protocols.done: Ongoing. Check it at each new goal.

protocols.name: Reading flow and resistance
protocols.when: When you’re unsure whether a goal, a path or a person is meant for you, or everything feels like pushing uphill.
steps: Hard and wrong aren’t the same thing. Effort you choose can still feel like flow. What you’re watching is the direction, not the difficulty.
Look for the signs of flow: doors open, people say yes, things line up, you lose track of time, and your energy comes back even after hard days.
Look for the signs of resistance: every step is a fight, doors keep closing, the same block keeps showing up, and it drains you more than it gives.
Give it a fair run before you read it. One bad week isn’t a pattern. Look back over 2 to 4 weeks.
Read people the same way. The people meant for you tend to feel easy to be around, even in hard conversations. Constant friction with someone is information.
If it’s mostly flow, lean in. Put more of your time and energy where things open up.
If it’s non-stop resistance, ask what it’s telling you: not this, not now, or not this way. Then use the Price check to choose.
Follow the open door. Sometimes what’s meant for you is the thing that keeps showing up while you’re pushing on something else.
signals: You’re unsure whether a goal, path or person is right.
Every step feels like pushing uphill.
protocols.start: Start the flow log.
protocols.deeper: After 2 to 4 weeks, read the pattern, then lean in, or choose with the Price check.
working: You can say where things flow and where you’re forcing.
protocols.done: After a clear read. Then whenever a path or person feels off.

protocols.name: The pause before yes
protocols.when: When you say yes too fast to keep someone happy, before you realize what it will cost you, especially when your own cup is already empty.
steps: Notice the urge to say yes on the spot. A fast yes to keep the peace is a habit, not a decision.
Buy time: “Let me check and get back to you.” A real yes can wait an hour.
Check your cup: is your time, energy or money full, half or empty right now?
Ask the price: what will this yes actually cost you, and what will you have to say no to because of it?
Choose on purpose: yes, a smaller yes, a later, or a kind no.
If it’s a no, keep it short and kind. You don’t owe a long explanation.
It’s okay to change a yes you gave too fast. Go back early and offer what you can actually do.
Filling your own cup first isn’t selfish. It’s how you keep having something to give.
signals: You’re overcommitted, or mention saying yes to things you didn’t want.
Your cup is empty most days.
protocols.start: “Let me get back to you”, and check your cup.
protocols.deeper: A smaller yes, and changing one yes you gave too fast.
working: Fewer regretted yeses.
More of your time goes to your goal.
protocols.done: When pausing before yes is automatic.

protocols.name: Your own agency
protocols.when: When you keep pleasing people who take advantage of you, or act differently than you normally would when a certain person or thing is around.
steps: Notice where you shrink: with whom, or around what, do you stop doing what you’d normally do or say?
Name what you would do if they weren’t there. That’s your own agency talking.
Check whether it flows both ways. Do they give as well as take? Is your no respected, or argued with until it turns into a yes?
Watch for the signs of being taken advantage of: guilt used to move you, help that only goes one way, and plans that always run on their terms.
Take one small act of agency in their presence: order what you want, say what you think, leave when you’re ready.
Set one clear boundary, and decide what you’ll do if it isn’t respected.
Let them be disappointed. Someone else’s disappointment isn’t your emergency.
Tell someone in your circle what you’re changing. Agency is easier with backup.
protocols.safety: If you feel unsafe saying no to someone, or they control your money, where you go or who you see, that isn’t a boundary to solve alone. Reach out to someone you trust, a counselor, or a domestic violence hotline. If you’re in danger, call your local emergency number.
signals: You describe someone taking advantage, or acting differently around a person.
Your no keeps turning into a yes.
protocols.start: Where do I shrink?, and the two-way check.
protocols.deeper: One act of agency in your presence, and one boundary with a clear consequence.
working: You do what you’d normally do, even with that person around.
protocols.done: When you can stay yourself around that person, or have chosen distance.

protocols.name: Learning to say no
protocols.when: When saying no feels hard, scary or rude, so you say yes to things you don’t want, can’t afford, or don’t have room for.
steps: No is a full sentence, and a kind no is still a no.
Start small. Write a “no ladder” from easiest to hardest, and practice on the easy ones first: a waiter, a sales call, one extra task.
Say no to the thing, not the person: “I can’t take this on, and I appreciate you asking.”
Keep it short. The more you explain, the more there is to argue with.
If they push, say it again, calmly, with the same words.
Expect a guilt wave afterward. Feel it, and don’t take the no back.
Notice what your no made room for: time, rest, your goal.
Say no to yourself too: to the old habit, the extra scroll, the late night that costs you tomorrow.
signals: You say saying no feels rude, mean or scary.
protocols.start: Write the no ladder, and say the easiest no.
protocols.deeper: Climb the ladder, repeat calmly under pushback, and ride the guilt wave.
working: Your nos get shorter, and the guilt passes faster.
protocols.done: When a no doesn’t need a speech.

protocols.name: Speaking up for yourself
protocols.when: When you swallow what you think or need, go along to avoid conflict, or hint instead of asking.
steps: Notice the moment you swallow it: the thought you didn’t say, the need you didn’t mention.
Start where it’s easy. Speak up in low-stakes moments first: a wrong order, the seat you want, your take on a movie.
Use “I” statements: “I see it differently.” “I need a day to think.” “I’d prefer…”
Say it early, while it’s small. Swallowed things grow.
Keep your voice calm and your words simple. You don’t have to be loud to be clear.
Ask for what you need directly instead of hinting.
If it comes out wobbly, it still counts. You can circle back: “I want to say that more clearly.”
Not everyone will like it. The people meant for you will respect it.
signals: You swallow your opinions, or hint instead of asking.
protocols.start: One true sentence in a low-stakes moment.
protocols.deeper: “I” statements in harder moments, and asking directly.
working: You say what you think more days than not.
protocols.done: When speaking up feels normal, not brave.

protocols.name: Your worth, held
protocols.when: When you doubt yourself, feel you have to earn your place, or don’t believe you deserve what you’re asking for.
steps: Worth is held, not hyped. Telling yourself “I’m worthy” a hundred times moves less than keeping one small promise to yourself for twenty days.
Keep small promises to yourself. Every kept one is proof your gut can read.
Write your proof list: things you’ve done, handled, or made it through. Add to it every week.
Notice your inner critic. Write down what it says, then what you’d say to a friend who said that about themselves.
Drop the words that shrink you: “just”, “only”, “sorry”, “I’m no expert”.
Stop earning your worth by overgiving. Your value isn’t measured by what you do for others.
Take up space on purpose: let a compliment land, name your price, sit where you want to sit.
Measure yourself against who you were last month, not against someone else’s highlight reel.
protocols.safety: If your sense of worth is very low, or it comes with hopelessness, talk to a counselor or doctor. Worth can be rebuilt, and you don’t have to do it alone. If you’re in crisis, call your local emergency number or a crisis line now.
signals: You talk yourself down, or feel you have to earn your place.
Error thoughts about not being good enough.
protocols.start: Keep one small promise a day, and start a proof list.
protocols.deeper: Answer the critic, drop the shrink words, and name your price.
working: The proof list keeps growing.
You let compliments land.
protocols.done: Ongoing, quietly. Worth grows with every kept promise.

protocols.name: Catching error thoughts
protocols.when: When harsh thoughts or statements about yourself keep showing up, including ones you picked up from other people. Unlearning what you tell yourself.
steps: Watch for the moments. Old thoughts show up when you’re stuck, tired, comparing yourself, or something goes wrong.
Catch it as it happens. Notice the exact words: “I’m stupid.” “I always mess this up.” “People like me don’t get that.”
Name it, out loud or in your head: “Error thought.” Naming it puts space between you and it.
Ask whose voice it is. Many of these started as something someone else said to you. You don’t have to keep carrying it.
Flip it to the inverse, in words you can believe. “I’m stupid” becomes “This is tough, but I’ll figure it out.”
Make the flip true, not fake. If the full opposite feels like a lie, use a bridge: “I’m learning this.” “I’m getting better at this.”
Back it up with one small action. Your gut believes what you do, so the action is what makes the new thought stick.
Catch what you say out loud too. “I’m terrible with money” in a conversation is an error statement. Correct it mid-sentence.
Keep an error log. Within a few weeks you’ll see the same few error thoughts repeat, and you’ll catch them faster.
signals: You write harsh things about yourself in check-ins: “I’m stupid”, “I always mess up”.
protocols.start: Catch it and say “error thought”. Flipping can come later.
protocols.deeper: Flip it, ask whose voice it is, back it up with action, and keep the log.
working: You catch error thoughts faster, and the same ones show up less.
protocols.done: When catching and flipping happens on its own most of the time.

protocols.name: Your five: the family you’re building
protocols.when: When you want to grow, and the people closest to you shape what feels normal. The few people you spend the most time with shape your habits, moods and chances. Research on social networks shows habits like exercise, eating, smoking and even happiness spread between people who are close, and we naturally mirror the people around us most.
steps: Map your five: the people you spend the most time and contact with, in person, on the phone and online.
For each one, notice what you pick up from them: habits, moods, and how you both talk about money, work, your body and your future. We mirror the people closest to us, the good and the bad.
Ask of each: does time with them pull me toward my goal, or away from it? Do I leave amplified, drained, or neutral?
Name the people you want more of: people already living part of what you want, who make you better just by being around them.
Grow your circle on purpose. Spend more time where those people are: groups, classes, communities, work. (See “Opening doors”.)
Rebalance, don’t purge. A little less time with the people who drain you, a little more with the people who amplify you. Distance comes before goodbye.
Be the friend you want to have. Bring the habits, encouragement and honesty you’re looking for. Like attracts like.
Build your chosen family: the few people who show up, tell you the truth, and want you to win. Invest in them on purpose.
Check your five every few months. As you change, your circle will change too, and that’s part of growing.
signals: You describe the people around you pulling you back.
Your goal needs a different crowd.
protocols.start: Map your five.
protocols.deeper: Rebalance one hour a week, be in the room, and invest in chosen family.
working: You spend more time with people who amplify you.
protocols.done: Check every few months.

protocols.name: Four ways to stay clear
protocols.when: For everyday life, especially in hard moments with other people: mean what you say, your world not your worth, ask don’t guess, and your best for the day you have.
steps: Mean what you say. Your word counts: say what you mean, keep your promises, and don’t use words against yourself or anyone else. (See “Be precise” and “Catching error thoughts”.)
Their world, not your worth. What people say and do mostly comes from what they’re carrying, not from your value.
When something stings, pause before you react and ask: is this about me, or about their world?
Ask, don’t guess. Instead of filling in the blanks, ask: “What did you mean by that?”
Say what you want clearly, so other people don’t have to guess either.
Your best, for the day you have. Your best changes day to day, and a hard-day best still counts. No guilt, no burnout.
At night, check in: Did I mean what I said? Did I let someone else’s words or mood decide how I felt about myself? Did I guess instead of asking? Did I give my best for the day I had?
signals: Conflict, hurt feelings or misunderstandings in your check-ins.
protocols.start: The evening check, once a day.
protocols.deeper: Practice one of the four on purpose each week.
working: Fewer arguments from guesses, and less taking things to heart.
protocols.done: Always on, as a nightly habit.

protocols.name: The comeback
protocols.when: When you’ve fallen off completely: a lost week, a lost month, or longer.
steps: Welcome back. No shame and no catch-up debt. Starting again is the skill.
Don’t audit the gap. Skip the guilt review; all you need is the next step.
Restart with the small version of your step for three days.
Ask one question about the gap: what pulled me away? Write one line, then move on.
Remove one thing that made falling off easy.
Tell one person you’re back, if that helps you stay.
Count from today. How fast you come back matters more than any streak.
signals: No check-ins for a week or more, and then you return.
protocols.start: The small version for three days.
protocols.deeper: Remove one easy exit, and tell someone you’re back.
working: You come back faster after each gap.
protocols.done: After a week of steps. Then back to the normal plan.

protocols.name: Body basics: fuel your steam
protocols.when: When low energy, poor sleep or skipped meals keep shrinking your steam.
steps: Your steam starts in your body. Sleep, movement, food and water come before willpower.
Sleep: pick one thing that helps you rest, like a set wind-down time or the phone out of the bedroom.
Move a little every day, any way you enjoy. A ten-minute walk counts.
Eat something real before you run on empty. Regular meals beat perfect ones.
Drink water before coffee.
Get outside and see daylight early in the day.
Change one basic at a time, and notice what it does for your steam.
protocols.safety: This is everyday care, not medical advice. For ongoing exhaustion, sleep problems, pain, or big changes to food or exercise, talk to a doctor.
signals: You mention poor sleep, exhaustion or skipped meals.
Low steam most days for a week.
protocols.start: One basic, usually sleep or a daily walk.
protocols.deeper: Add one basic at a time, and notice the effect on your steam.
working: More good or okay days, fewer hard ones.
protocols.done: When the basics run in the background. Check once a month.

protocols.name: Big life changes
protocols.when: During a move, a breakup, a job loss, a new baby, an illness or a loss, when life itself has become the big goal.
steps: Big changes take energy, even the good ones. Lower the bar on purpose.
Switch your plan to gentle mode: small versions, fewer of them, more rest.
Keep one small anchor that’s the same every day: a walk, a meal, a call.
Let yourself feel it. Grief, fear and relief can all show up at once.
Lean on your circle, and ask for specific help: a meal, a ride, a call.
Put big decisions on hold where you can, until the ground feels steadier.
When you’re ready, ask what this change makes room for. That can become your next goal.
protocols.safety: Grief and big changes can weigh a lot. If you’re struggling to get through the day, or feel hopeless, talk to a counselor or doctor. In a crisis, call your local emergency number or a crisis line.
signals: You mention a move, a breakup, a job loss, an illness, a new baby or a death.
protocols.start: Gentle mode, and one anchor.
protocols.deeper: Ask for specific help. When you’re ready, what this change makes room for.
working: You get through the days with some steadiness.
protocols.done: When the ground feels steadier. Then ease back into the normal plan.

protocols.name: What you actually value
protocols.when: When you’re not sure your goal is truly yours, or it feels like someone else’s dream.
steps: Ask: whose goal is this? Mine, my family’s, my friends’, or my feed’s?
List the moments you felt most like yourself. What was true in each one?
Pull your values out of those moments: freedom, family, craft, adventure, peace, whatever shows up.
Pick your top three.
Check your goal against them. Does it serve at least one? Does it cost one you care about?
Adjust the goal, or keep it with clearer reasons why.
Revisit your values once or twice a year. They change as you do.
signals: You say your goal doesn’t feel like yours.
Strong resistance with no clear reason.
protocols.start: Whose goal is it?
protocols.deeper: Find your top three values, and check the goal against you.
working: You can say why your goal matters to you, in your own words.
protocols.done: Once the goal is checked. Revisit once or twice a year.

protocols.name: Your signal: feel it, hold it, live it
protocols.when: At the heart of every goal. What you hold in your gut most of the day is your signal. Words and wishes don’t change it; feelings faced and actions taken do.
steps: Your signal is what you hold, not what you say. Repeating words over a feeling you don’t have hides the feeling instead of changing it.
Feel the future fully. Picture an ordinary day once your goal is real, in first person, as if it’s already true. Notice how it feels in your body.
Notice the gap. What shows up right after? Doubt, fear, “that’s not for me”. That’s the other half. Don’t cover it; feel it.
Ask yourself the question that fits: what it’ll really cost you to get what you want, whether there’s a hidden upside to not having it yet, or what would scare you about getting it.
Choose one feeling from that future to hold today: calm, steady, enough. Held, not high. A spike fades; a baseline changes things.
Live it in one small way. Make one choice today that the version of you who already has it would make. Action teaches your body the future is normal.
Check your signal at 2:47. Are you holding it, or did old feelings take over? No shame. Come back to it.
Notice what’s moving: doors opening, people showing up, small signs. Be grateful for what’s already on its way.
Let go of the how and the when. Hold the feeling, take the step, and loosen your grip on the rest.

lens.energy: For people who see it as energy: everything is energy, like attracts like, and you are a broadcaster and receiver of what you feel. Your signal is your frequency, and the steps tune it.
lens.mind: For people who see it as psychology: what you feel shapes what you notice, what you choose and how others respond to you. Your signal is your baseline, and the steps shift it.

signals: Every goal, from the start.
Your check-ins show you wanting it but feeling far from it, or trying to think your way there with words alone.
protocols.start: Live it for two minutes, and name the gap.
protocols.deeper: Hold one feeling each day, live it once a day, check your signal at 2:47, and release the how.
working: Your 2:47 checks show the feeling holding more often.
You notice doors and signs, and act on you.
protocols.done: Never done. It’s the background of every goal; it just gets steadier.

protocols.name: Navigating your emotions
protocols.when: When a big feeling hits, or the same heavy feeling keeps coming back and pulls you away from your goal.
steps: Name it, as exactly as you can: not “bad”, but “disappointed”, “embarrassed”, “scared I’m too late”. Naming a feeling takes some of its power.
Find it in your body: the tight chest, the knot in your stomach, the heat in your face.
Feel it fully for a minute or two, without fixing it. Feelings move through faster when you let them.
Ask what it’s telling you. Fear often points at something that matters. Anger often points at a boundary.
Move one step up, not ten. From hopeless to frustrated, from frustrated to hopeful. Pick the next feeling you can actually believe.
Act from the new feeling, in one small way.
If it’s an old heavy feeling that keeps coming back, notice what sets it off, and use “Catching error thoughts” on the thought that rides with it.
Don’t bottle it and don’t fake it. Felt and moved through beats pushed down and covered up.
protocols.safety: If a feeling is too big to move through, or it stays for weeks, talk to someone you trust or a counselor. If you feel unsafe or hopeless, call your local emergency number or a crisis line now.
signals: You describe a big feeling, or the same heavy feeling for days.
Your check-ins swing from very high to very low.
protocols.start: Name it exactly, and find it in your body.
protocols.deeper: Feel it fully, hear what it’s telling you, move one step up, and act from there.
working: You name feelings more exactly.
Big feelings pass faster, without being bottled up.
protocols.done: When moving through a feeling is something you know how to do.

protocols.name: Keeping your power
protocols.when: When you believe someone else holds all the keys, or that you have to do it exactly the way someone else did. Also when you’re taking advice from mentors, coaches, books or courses.
steps: Notice where you hand your power over: “I can’t until they…”, “If I just find the right coach, course or person…”, “I have to do it exactly like they did.”
No one holds all the keys. People can open doors and share what worked for them, but your path won’t look like theirs.
There’s no single right way. Everyone is different: a different life, timing, set of strengths and starting point.
Learn from people who’ve done it, and keep your hands on the wheel. Advice is input, not orders.
Run advice through your gut. What resonates? Keep it. What feels off? Leave it, without needing to argue about it.
Test a piece of advice as a Try, not a rule. See whether it works for you before you make it yours.
Be careful with anyone who says theirs is the only way, or makes you feel you can’t do it without them.
Take credit for your own progress. When something works, notice what you did.
That includes this app. Take what fits, change what doesn’t, and trust yourself.
protocols.safety: If a coach, group or person pressures you to keep paying more, to cut off the people close to you, or to hand over control of your choices to keep your progress, step back and talk it through with someone you trust.
signals: You say you can’t move until someone else does something.
You’re following someone’s method to the letter and it isn’t working for you.
You mention a coach, course or mentor as the answer.
protocols.start: Where did I hand it over? and Take what resonates.
protocols.deeper: Advice as a Try, write your own way, and take back one key.
working: You talk about advice as input, not rules.
You take credit for what works.
protocols.done: When you trust your own read first and use advice to sharpen it.

protocols.name: Making room: letting go of the old to let the new in
protocols.when: When you’re holding on to something that’s already over: an old chapter, an old version of yourself, an old hurt, or something you’ve put years into. You can’t fully take in the new while your hands are full of the old.
steps: Name what you’re still carrying: a role, a label, a story, a hurt, a hope, a thing you keep paying for. Write it down. Seeing it is the first loosening.
Honor it before you release it. Write what it gave you, and thank it. Letting go isn’t pretending it didn’t matter.
Retire one old label. “I’m the responsible one.” “I’m not a creative person.” Write who you’re becoming instead, in words you can believe.
Stop paying for the past. If you wouldn’t start it today, ask what keeping it costs you now. Years already spent aren’t a reason to spend more.
Forgive to free yourself. Forgiving isn’t excusing what happened or letting someone back in. It’s putting down a weight you’ve been carrying for them.
Let grief come. Even the right goodbye can hurt. Feel it in small doses, then go back to your day.
Leave the space open for a while. Don’t rush to fill it with something that looks like the old thing. Notice what starts to show up.
After 7 days, look back: what feels lighter, and what wants to come in?
protocols.safety: If what you’re holding on to involves abuse, trauma or a deep loss, you don’t have to work through it alone. Talk to someone you trust or a professional. Forgiving someone never means staying somewhere unsafe. If you’re in crisis, call your local emergency number or a crisis line now.
signals: You keep going back to how things used to be, or who you used to be.
You describe a grudge, a regret or an old story that still stings.
You’re staying in something mostly because of what you’ve already put into it.
protocols.start: Week 1: name what you’re carrying, and honor it. Nothing has to go yet.
protocols.deeper: Week 2 on: retire one label, stop paying for one thing, and leave the space open. Forgiveness when you’re ready, not before.
working: You talk about the old chapter in the past tense, with less charge.
You notice something new showing up in the space you made.
protocols.done: When the old thing comes up and doesn’t pull you back. You can remember it without living in it.
